questions.stem: Which finding is the most reliable indicator of fluid retention in a client with heart failure?

options.text: Weight gain of 2 kg (4.4 lb) in 2 days

rationale.correct: Daily weight is the best measure of fluid balance in heart failure.

perOption.a: Rapid weight gain is the most sensitive sign of fluid retention; 1 kg is about 1 L of fluid.
perOption.b: Fatigue is nonspecific.
perOption.c: A mildly fast heart rate has many causes.
perOption.d: Thirst doesn't reliably show fluid retention.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the best indicator of fluid retention in heart failure.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with heart failure about self-care at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weigh yourself every morning after urinating, before breakfast, on the same scale
Report a gain of more than 1 to 1.5 kg (2 to 3 lb) in a day or 2 kg (5 lb) in a week
Limit sodium as prescribed, often to about 2,000 mg a day
Use a salt substitute to flavor food
Report increasing shortness of breath or needing more pillows to sleep
Skip your diuretic on days you feel well

rationale.correct: Heart failure self-care: daily weights, sodium limits, taking medications consistently and recognizing early warning signs.

perOption.a: Consistent timing makes daily weights comparable.
perOption.b: These gains signal fluid retention that needs treatment adjustment.
perOption.c: Sodium causes fluid retention.
perOption.d: Most salt substitutes contain potassium and can cause hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors, ARBs or spironolactone.
perOption.e: Worsening dyspnea or orthopnea signals decompensation.
perOption.f: Diuretics are taken as prescribed to prevent fluid buildup.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach heart failure self-management.

questions.stem: A client comes to the emergency department with shortness of breath. The B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is 980 pg/mL. What does this result suggest?

rationale.correct: BNP rises with ventricular stretch and helps identify heart failure as the cause of dyspnea.

perOption.a: BNP is released when the ventricles are stretched; a level above about 400 pg/mL strongly suggests heart failure.
perOption.b: Pneumonia doesn't markedly raise BNP.
perOption.c: BNP helps tell cardiac causes of dyspnea from lung causes like asthma.
perOption.d: A normal BNP is below 100 pg/mL.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with acute pulmonary edema is extremely short of breath, with pink frothy sputum. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: High Fowler's with the legs dependent

rationale.correct: Upright with legs dependent reduces preload and improves lung expansion.

perOption.a: This increases venous return and worsens the pulmonary congestion.
perOption.b: Sitting upright with the legs down reduces venous return and eases breathing.
perOption.c: This doesn't reduce preload.
perOption.d: Head-down positioning worsens pulmonary edema.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is switching from lisinopril to sacubitril/valsartan. Lisinopril was last taken this morning. When can the first dose of sacubitril/valsartan be given?

options.text: At least 36 hours after the last lisinopril dose
Only after a normal potassium level

rationale.correct: An ACE inhibitor and an ARNI must never overlap; separate them by 36 hours.

perOption.a: Taking the two together raises the risk of angioedema.
perOption.b: A 36-hour washout is required between an ACE inhibitor and sacubitril/valsartan to reduce the risk of angioedema.
perOption.c: A week isn't required.
perOption.d: Potassium is monitored, but the washout period is the key rule.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply the washout rule when switching from an ACE inhibitor to sacubitril/valsartan.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure takes spironolactone and lisinopril. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor most closely?

rationale.correct: Spironolactone (a potassium-sparing diuretic) and ACE inhibitors both raise potassium.

perOption.a: Both drugs keep potassium in the body, so the risk of hyperkalemia is high.
perOption.b: Calcium isn't significantly affected.
perOption.c: Glucose isn't the main concern.
perOption.d: Hemoglobin isn't the main concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor potassium with potassium-sparing drug combinations.

content.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{b1}}, and the nurse should anticipate a prescription for {{b2}}.

rationale.correct: Missing diuretic doses often triggers heart failure exacerbations. Treatment focuses on diuresis and reducing preload.

perOption.b1:a: Weight gain, crackles, orthopnea and edema after missing the diuretic show fluid overload.
perOption.b1:b: There's no fever or productive cough to suggest infection.
perOption.b1:c: The findings show fluid excess, not deficit.
perOption.b2:a: A loop diuretic removes excess fluid quickly.
perOption.b2:b: Extra fluid would worsen the overload.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

exhibits.body: A 70-year-old with heart failure ran out of furosemide 5 days ago. Weight is up 2.7 kg (6 lb) since last week. Sleeps on 3 pillows. Crackles in both lung bases; 2+ ankle edema. Temperature 36.8 °C; SpO2 91% on room air.

questions.stem: A client is bleeding after surgery. Which finding is the earliest sign of hypovolemic shock?

options.text: Blood pressure falling from 128/76 to 84/50 mm Hg
Heart rate rising from 82/min to 108/min with restlessness

rationale.correct: In early shock, compensation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction, anxiety) keeps blood pressure normal; hypotension appears late.

perOption.a: Hypotension is a later sign that appears after compensation fails.
perOption.b: Tachycardia and restlessness come early as the body compensates.
perOption.c: Very low urine output reflects established poor perfusion.
perOption.d: Mottling is a late sign.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize early compensated shock.

questions.stem: For each client finding, indicate the type of shock it is most consistent with.

rows.text: Flat neck veins and falling hemoglobin after a gastrointestinal bleed
Crackles, distended neck veins and an S3 after a large anterior MI
Temperature 39.4 °C (103 °F), warm flushed skin and WBC 18,000/mm3
Blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg with a rising troponin after chest pain
Severe burns over 40% of the body with low urine output

rationale.correct: Hypovolemic = low volume (flat veins); cardiogenic = pump failure (congestion); septic = infection with vasodilation (warm skin early).

perOption.r1:c1: Blood loss reduces circulating volume, so the neck veins flatten.
perOption.r1:c2: Cardiogenic shock causes distended neck veins.
perOption.r2:c1: Volume loss doesn't cause crackles or JVD.
perOption.r2:c2: A failing ventricle backs fluid into the lungs and veins.
perOption.r2:c3: Septic shock doesn't typically cause an S3 or JVD.
perOption.r3:c1: Hypovolemic shock causes cool, pale skin.
perOption.r3:c2: Cardiogenic shock causes cool, clammy skin.
perOption.r3:c3: Infection with vasodilation causes warm skin early in septic shock.
perOption.r4:c1: There's no fluid or blood loss.
perOption.r4:c2: Pump failure after MI causes cardiogenic shock.
perOption.r4:c3: There are no signs of infection.
perOption.r5:c1: Burn injury shifts large volumes of plasma out of the vessels.
perOption.r5:c2: Pump function isn't the primary problem.
perOption.r5:c3: There's no infection at this stage.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish types of shock by their findings.

questions.stem: A client with suspected sepsis has a prescription for IV piperacillin-tazobactam. What should the nurse do before starting the antibiotic?

options.text: Wait for the complete blood count results

rationale.correct: Sepsis bundle: measure lactate, draw blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, and give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or a lactate of 4 mmol/L or higher.

perOption.a: Cultures are drawn before antibiotics so the organism can be identified, but antibiotics shouldn't be delayed.
perOption.b: Waiting delays lifesaving antibiotics.
perOption.c: Treating fever doesn't come before cultures and antibiotics.
perOption.d: A catheter isn't required before antibiotics.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Follow the sepsis bundle order.

questions.stem: A client with septic shock who weighs 70 kg is prescribed a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus. How many mL should the client receive?

rationale.correct: Volume = 30 mL/kg × 70 kg = 2,100 mL.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a weight-based fluid bolus.

questions.stem: Minutes after eating peanuts, a client has hives, wheezing, throat tightness and a blood pressure of 80/48 mm Hg. Which medication should the nurse give first?

options.text: Epinephrine 0.3 to 0.5 mg IM into the anterolateral thigh

rationale.correct: Epinephrine IM is the first drug for anaphylaxis; repeat every 5 to 15 minutes as needed.

perOption.a: Epinephrine reverses bronchospasm and vasodilation and is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
perOption.b: Antihistamines are second-line and don't treat airway swelling or shock.
perOption.c: Steroids act slowly and are adjuncts.
perOption.d: Albuterol helps wheezing but doesn't treat shock or airway edema.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Give the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: Four hours after cardiac surgery, a client's chest tube drainage suddenly drops from 100 mL/hr to almost none. The blood pressure is 78/56 mm Hg, the neck veins are distended and the heart sounds are muffled. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds) signals tamponade; prepare for pericardiocentesis or return to surgery.

perOption.a: Hypotension, JVD and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) after a sudden drop in drainage suggest blood collecting around the heart.
perOption.b: Hypovolemia causes flat, not distended, neck veins.
perOption.c: Pneumothorax causes absent breath sounds on one side, not muffled heart sounds.
perOption.d: PE doesn't cause muffled heart sounds.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cardiac tamponade.

questions.stem: Which finding is most consistent with acute pericarditis?

options.text: Chest pain that eases when the client sits up and leans forward
Chest pain that radiates to the left arm with exertion

rationale.correct: Pericarditis: sharp, pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, with a pericardial friction rub.

perOption.a: Leaning forward pulls the inflamed pericardium away from the heart and eases the pain.
perOption.b: This suggests angina.
perOption.c: This suggests ischemia.
perOption.d: This suggests peripheral arterial disease.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the signs of pericarditis.

questions.stem: A client with a history of injection drug use is admitted with suspected infective endocarditis. Which findings support this diagnosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Painless red spots on the palms and soles (Janeway lesions)
Pericardial friction rub relieved by leaning forward

rationale.correct: Endocarditis shows fever, a new murmur and embolic signs (splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots).

perOption.a: Fever is the most common finding in endocarditis.
perOption.b: Vegetations damage the valves and cause new murmurs.
perOption.c: These come from small emboli.
perOption.d: These are emboli to the skin.
perOption.e: A barrel chest is associated with COPD.
perOption.f: A friction rub points to pericarditis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize signs of infective endocarditis.

questions.stem: A client has had a mechanical mitral valve replacement. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take warfarin for the rest of my life."
"I'll tell my dentist about my valve before any dental work."
"I can stop the warfarin once the incision heals."

rationale.correct: Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin with INR monitoring and endocarditis prophylaxis.

perOption.a: Mechanical valves need lifelong anticoagulation.
perOption.b: Clients with prosthetic valves need antibiotic prophylaxis before some dental procedures.
perOption.c: Stopping warfarin risks clots forming on the valve and stroke.
perOption.d: Regular INR checks are needed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with severe aortic stenosis reports chest pain. Which prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula if SpO2 is below 90%

rationale.correct: In severe aortic stenosis, vasodilators such as nitroglycerin must be used with great caution because they can cause a sharp fall in blood pressure.

perOption.a: Oxygen for hypoxemia is appropriate.
perOption.b: Clients with severe aortic stenosis depend on preload; nitrates can cause severe hypotension and syncope.
perOption.c: An ECG is appropriate for chest pain.
perOption.d: A troponin level is appropriate to assess for ischemia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the risk of nitrates in aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: A client has a blood pressure of 224/132 mm Hg with a severe headache and blurred vision. What is the goal for the first hour of treatment?

options.text: Lower the blood pressure to normal (below 120/80) as fast as possible
Lower the mean arterial pressure by no more than about 25%
Keep the blood pressure the same and treat the headache
Give oral medications and recheck tomorrow

rationale.correct: In a hypertensive emergency, reduce the MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then gradually toward 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours.

perOption.a: Lowering the pressure too fast can cause ischemia of the brain, heart and kidneys.
perOption.b: Gradual lowering protects organs used to high pressures.
perOption.c: End-organ damage needs treatment now.
perOption.d: A hypertensive emergency needs IV medication and close monitoring.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Set safe goals for treating a hypertensive emergency.

questions.stem: A client has been on an IV nitroprusside infusion for 3 days for a hypertensive emergency. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?

options.text: Confusion, metabolic acidosis and a smell of bitter almonds
IV bag covered with an opaque cover

rationale.correct: Nitroprusside breaks down into cyanide; watch for toxicity, protect the infusion from light and monitor blood pressure continuously.

perOption.a: This is an expected treatment response.
perOption.b: These suggest cyanide toxicity, a risk with prolonged or high-dose nitroprusside.
perOption.c: Nitroprusside is protected from light, so this is appropriate.
perOption.d: This heart rate is acceptable.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize nitroprusside toxicity.

questions.stem: A client is 3 hours past coronary artery bypass graft surgery. Which finding should the nurse report to the surgeon?

options.text: Mediastinal chest tube drainage of 150 mL/hr for the past 2 hours
Pain at the sternal incision rated 5 out of 10
Serosanguineous drainage in the chest tube

rationale.correct: Excessive chest tube drainage after cardiac surgery suggests bleeding and needs the surgeon's evaluation.

perOption.a: Drainage over 100 to 150 mL/hr for 2 hours or more suggests hemorrhage.
perOption.b: Mild hypothermia is common right after surgery and is treated with warming.
perOption.c: Moderate incision pain is expected.
perOption.d: Serosanguineous drainage is expected early.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize bleeding after cardiac surgery.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with Raynaud's phenomenon. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll wear gloves when I take things out of the freezer."
"I'll cut down to two cigarettes a day."

rationale.correct: Raynaud's teaching: avoid cold, nicotine, caffeine and stress, which all cause vasospasm.

perOption.a: Cold triggers vasospasm, so gloves are appropriate.
perOption.b: Any nicotine causes vasoconstriction; complete smoking cessation is needed.
perOption.c: Caffeine can cause vasoconstriction.
perOption.d: Stress can trigger attacks.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client with Raynaud's phenomenon.

questions.stem: A client with peripheral arterial disease is starting a walking program. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Walk until the pain starts, rest until it goes away, then walk again."
"Elevate your legs above heart level when resting."

rationale.correct: Walk to claudication, rest, repeat, for 30 to 45 minutes about 3 times a week.

perOption.a: Supervised walking to the point of claudication builds collateral circulation.
perOption.b: Exercise improves walking distance.
perOption.c: Elevation reduces arterial flow; legs should be level or dependent.
perOption.d: Compression can further reduce arterial flow.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach an exercise program for peripheral arterial disease.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a myocardial infarction asks when it's safe to resume sexual activity. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Usually once you can climb two flights of stairs without symptoms, but confirm with your provider."
"You'll need to avoid sexual activity permanently."
"Take sildenafil before activity to protect your heart."

rationale.correct: Many clients can resume sexual activity when they can tolerate moderate exertion, such as two flights of stairs, often 1 to 2 weeks after an uncomplicated MI.

perOption.a: Most clients can resume sooner.
perOption.b: Tolerating this level of exertion suggests sexual activity is likely safe.
perOption.c: This is inaccurate and harmful to quality of life.
perOption.d: Sildenafil doesn't protect the heart and is dangerous with nitrates.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The home health nurse documents a visit with a client who has heart failure. Highlight the findings that indicate worsening heart failure.

segments.text: "I had to sleep in my recliner the last two nights."
Weight is up 1.8 kg (4 lb) since 2 days ago.
New crackles in both lung bases.
Ate a frozen dinner and canned soup yesterday.

rationale.correct: Orthopnea, rapid weight gain and new crackles signal decompensation.

perOption.s2: Needing to sleep upright (orthopnea) signals worsening pulmonary congestion.
perOption.s4: Rapid weight gain shows fluid retention.
perOption.s8: Crackles show fluid in the lungs.
perOption.s10: This is a controlled blood pressure.
perOption.s12: High-sodium food is a risk factor to address, but it isn't itself a sign of worsening.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.
